anchors.fact: The Rickey (whiskey, half a lime, soda, ice, no sugar) caught on at Shoomaker's, a Washington, DC, bar known as "Shoo's", in the late 1880s, and from there spread through the city. It carried the name of a regular, the lobbyist Joe Rickey (Oxford RICKEY pdf 1661, 1663; *Imbibe!* pdf 118).
anchors.meaning: The loud name on the drink.

anchors.fact: Oxford names two people as the drink's popularizers, side by side: Rickey and the bar's head bartender, George Williamson (1849–1915), who worked there for much of the bar's life and had a long association with the drink (Oxford pdf 1661, 1663, SHOOMAKER'S pdf 1789). Wondrich has Rickey getting Williamson to start making them for him (*Imbibe!* pdf 117).
anchors.meaning: The steady one behind the bar is in the record beside the famous one.
anchors.speaksTo: Confidence; drivers: provide structure; Build connection

anchors.fact: In 1893 Rickey told the *New York Herald* he "was not the author" of the drink, only the man who brought it east, and gave an account of its origin that put it down to a friend in St. Louis. At least three of his accounts were published while he lived (Oxford pdf 1662–1663).
anchors.meaning: The famous name on the drink was himself the first to say the drink wasn't his invention.

anchors.fact: The tellings differ on the lime. In Rickey's own account, as Oxford relays it, he had used lemon, and the lime came in at Shoo's through one of the bartenders, "more than likely" Williamson. In a 1930 history by George Rothwell Brown, a stranger gave Williamson limes, and Williamson made one for Rickey, who is said to have approved (Oxford pdf 1663). Wondrich has lime from the start (*Imbibe!* pdf 118).
anchors.meaning: Told only as "the story goes": only Rickey's own telling puts the switch to lime on a bartender; in Brown's, a stranger hands Williamson the limes.

anchors.fact: In 1895 Rickey wrote out his recipe by hand for a Syracuse newspaper: a large glass, ice, whiskey or gin, lime juice, soda water (Oxford pdf 1662; *Imbibe!* pdf 118).
anchors.meaning: Whatever its origin, by then the lime was in the recipe the famous name wrote down himself.

anchors.fact: Shoomaker's sold whiskey under its own name, a rye that was often the base of the whiskey Rickey (Oxford pdf 1789). Rickey's own whiskey was reportedly a bourbon, Belle of Nelson, and the water he preferred, reportedly, was Apollinaris, a sparkling mineral water (Oxford pdf 1663).
anchors.meaning: The bar's whiskey, and the water the colonel was said to favour: one choice from each side.

anchors.fact: Whether or not Rickey drank it, his friends did, and they tied it to him; the name itself is put down to two friends who came back asking for "a Joe Rickey" (Oxford pdf 1663).
anchors.meaning: The friends kept ordering it by his name.

cocktail.closingLine: Lime first, no sugar, not a word. Next time, let them catch you laughing.
cocktail.glassware: large plain tumbler (about 350 ml), three ice cubes
method: Squeeze half a lime into a large tumbler, then drop the squeezed half in after the juice.
Add three ice cubes, then the rye.
Top up with the cold mineral water, poured gently so it keeps its bubbles. Stir once.
No sugar, and nothing on top.
cocktail.name: Don't Look at Me

recipe.note: half a normal-sized lime, squeezed; the squeezed half goes in too
recommended, plain (unflavoured), cold; or any plain sparkling mineral water with a noticeable mineral taste

cocktail.tagline: Your straight face brings out everyone else's funniest side.

reading.epigraph: Named after a regular, mixed by the bartender. The regular denied being its author.
whoYouAre: Everyone around you thinks the funny one is your friend: the one who waves both arms through every story, gets the order wrong on purpose and starts the singing. You're sitting beside them, saying very little. You let them run, then one quiet word, or just a look, and the whole table goes. They get the laugh. It comes off you. Most of them take you for the serious one, and you go along with it, since that's part of the act.

How much you're enjoying it is the bit you hide best. You'd never say it, but you need them to be ridiculous. Put you in a room where everyone behaves and you're bored within the hour. People think you put up with the loudest person at the table. You picked them. Your fear is being taken at face value, as the grown-up who doesn't get the joke. You get it before anyone. And that's a gift to everyone near you: next to you, they're at their funniest, because someone steady is there to play it against.
yours: By the end of 1889, at a Washington bar everyone called Shoo's, a new drink had caught on: whiskey, half a lime, soda water and ice, and no sugar at all. It carried the name of a regular, a lobbyist known as Colonel Joe Rickey, who, it's said, showed bartenders how to make it wherever he went. Mixing it was the head bartender, George Williamson, who worked there for years and stayed with the drink a long time.

Then the comedy starts. In 1893 Rickey told a New York paper that he wasn't the drink's author at all, and at least three of his own accounts of how it began were printed in his lifetime. A later writer named Williamson as the real inventor. Even the lime has its stories: in Rickey's own, the switch to lime came from one of the bartenders; in another, a stranger handed Williamson the limes. Whether or not Rickey drank it himself, his friends did, and ordered it by his name. And in 1895, when he wrote his recipe out by hand for a newspaper, the lime was in it.

George Williamson, I like to think, loved it, and heard each new version of how the drink started, said nothing, and poured it again. The colonel had the name and the stories. The bartender had the drink. It doesn't work without both of them, and the steady one knows that better than anyone. So do you. You don't want the name on it. You want the act to work, and the act works because of you.

The cocktail I've made for you is a Rickey, a renowned classic, made with whiskey, the way it caught on at Shoo's: long, very cold and bone dry. Each partner puts something in. From the bar, a straight rye, because Shoo's sold its own and it often went into this drink. From the colonel, his water: he reportedly preferred Apollinaris, a sparkling mineral water, and I like to think it makes the lime taste a little brighter. The half lime belongs to both of them, whoever started it. The water is there as a nod to him, and the rye to the bar where Williamson poured, because I couldn't make it with only one of them.

You give everyone their best moment, and the one person nobody's watching is you. Once in a while, let it show. Let the loudest person at the table see you laugh. They've been playing to you from the start, and your laugh is the one they wanted most. The act survives it. They'll know you were having fun all along, and you get to have it with them, out in the open.
